chapter: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
title: Vaudeville, white tap dancers and Bojangles at the Palace
summary: Green recalls vaudeville ending in 1935 at the Palace, the white tap stars of the day, and the contest Bill Robinson won.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: It was on the rise. It was the most happy medium, tap dancing, see, because I mean Bojangles, he hadn't become the champion yet. He hadn't got into this at the Palace Theater, see? I mean there was vaudeville was here then, too. In the '30's. Vaudeville didn't go out until 1935. That was buried at the Palace Theater on Broadway, which was right there at -- where is that, 47th and Broadway -- and 7th Avenue, right? Now, see these tap dancers, you had people like Tom Patricola (PHONETIC), James Barton, Walter Huston and George Murphy --
Yeah, Buddy Ebsen. They was known tap dancers. Yeah. And there was a fellow -- yeah, and what you call -- yeah, that was about it. You see? Yes, that was it.

And they were playing in shows, like around here -- down there on Broadway, you see? They was in shows. But tap dancing itself, like Bojangles had been discovered by a millionaire, Marty Fawkins (PHONETIC), and he was just handled by Marty Fawkins exclusively. No other entertainer he had but Bojangles Robinson. He was playing at the Palace Theater. And this thing came about that they had all these white dancers, tap dancers, to settle what they called who was the best of the tap dancers, you know, that were supposed to be alive at that time. And George M. Cohan, of course, right? So they had a day of it at the Palace Theater, and Walter Winchell was alive. He was a famous columnist, you see, and he wrote about the show, see, and he said something about the dark horse won, you know, orchids. He had orchids to the dark horse won. That was Bill Bojangles Robinson. So from then on, I mean, tap dancing was on the rise, getting popular and popular and so forth, and I mean Mr. Cohan, I think he passed sometime after that, George M. And so did another one, he went away. Tom Patricola.
What I'm trying to get at is what was tap dancing then? Was it very popular? Was a lot of it being done in New York? Was it done on Broadway?
I said that. It was on the rise. That means, see, you know -- it was getting -- it was the most happy --
